If the thermostat fails, it will fail in the closed position. This is stated directly in [3] (TM-9-8000-principles-of-automotive-vehicles-1985.pdf, p.241): "The bellows-type thermostat is little used in modern equipment because it is sensitive to the pressure around it, making it inaccurate in modern pressurized cooling systems." Additionally, [3] states: "The liquid in the bellows vaporizes as the coolant is heated, causing the bellows to expand. The bellows pull the valve open as they expand, allowing coolant to circulate." This indicates that when functioning correctly, the thermostat opens (or fails to close) due to expansion of the bellows.

However, [3] also mentions: "The bellows-type thermostat is little used in modern equipment because it is sensitive to the pressure around it, making it inaccurate in modern pressurized cooling systems." This suggests that if a bellows-type thermostat does fail, it will likely remain open (or not close) due to its sensitivity to pressure changes. Therefore, based on these excerpts, if the thermostat fails, it would typically be in an open position rather than closed.

Single acting shock absorbers are designed such that they only generate damping force during spring rebound, not during spring deflection. They are attached in a way to ensure the damping force isn't generated during spring deflection. Their main disadvantage is that they provide damping only part of the time, requiring stiffer springs in the system and causing a slight preload on the suspension spring which can stiffen it out of proportion for mild terrain irregularities.

Double acting shock absorbers generate damping force both during spring compression as well as during rebound. They allow the use of softer suspension springs and enable optimal damping in both directions. In most cases, the damping force developed by double-acting shock absorbers during spring compression is much lower than that developed during rebound. This is desirable because a high damping force during spring compression would have the same effect on impact isolation as a very stiff spring; it would transmit the shock to the vehicle body, causing it to displace vertically.

[2] and [3] provide detailed explanations of these two types of shock absorbers.

Damping on rebound only forces the use of stiffer springs due to their design. Single acting shock absorbers provide damping only during spring rebound, not during deflection. This results in a requirement for softer suspension springs to achieve optimal performance and dampening effects [2]. However, this also leads to disadvantages such as requiring stiffer springs to maintain proper vehicle behavior on mild terrain irregularities due to the slight preload experienced by the suspension spring from the shock absorber return spring [2].

The relationship between indicated horsepower (IPH) and brake horsepower (BHP) is explained in [2] and [3]. In [2], it states that given the brake-horsepower formula, torque can be substituted into the formula because it is equal to the length of the arm times the scale reading. This yields a formula showing a direct torque-horsepower-speed relationship: Torque x RPM = 5,254 Btu's. In [3], it mentions that mechanical efficiency within the engine is the relationship between the actual power produced in the engine (Indicated horsepower) and the actual power delivered at the crankshaft (brake or shaft horsepower). The actual power at the crankshaft is always less than the power produced within the engine, due to frictional losses. Therefore, the relationship can be calculated by dividing brake or shaft horsepower by indicated horsepower.

[2] provides a formula that shows torque and speed are related to horsepower, indicating they are all dependent on each other. [3] further elaborates this dependency by stating that actual power at the crankshaft (BHP) is less than the power produced within the engine (IPH), which is due to frictional losses. Thus, the relationship between BHP and IPH can be summarized as: BHP < IPH.

A vibrating current regulator consists of a soft iron core, a heavy winding or current coil around the core, a set of regulator contact points normally held closed by spring tension, and a resistance unit connected across the two regulator contact points. [1]

The regulator stops the generator from exceeding its rated output by adjusting the resistance in the shunt-field circuit. For a vibrating current regulator, this is achieved by intermittently cutting a resistance in and out of the shunt-field circuit as the regulator contact points open and close due to varying magnetic pull of the core. This resistance is connected across the two regulator contact points when they are closed, preventing any further increase of output beyond the generator's rated maximum.

For a voltage regulator, it uses the amount of charge in the battery to control the output of the generator. When the generator reaches a speed at which it develops the regulated voltage, there will be no further increase in voltage with increasing speed. The voltage is maintained constant at all loads and at all higher speeds. If the spring tension of the regulator is adjusted appropriately, the maximum possible charging current remains constant for any one setting of the regulator, regardless of the condition of the battery.

In summary, both types of regulators ensure that the generator output does not exceed its rated value by either cutting resistance or adjusting the magnetic pull and spring pressure.

A diesel engine compresses the fuel and air mixture to about one-twentieth of its original volume. In contrast, a gasoline engine compresses the mixture to about one-eighth of its original volume [2]. This indicates that the diesel engine needs to compress the mixture more tightly to generate enough heat for ignition, as compared to the gasoline engine which mixes the fuel and air before reaching the combustion chamber.

A diesel engine needs no ignition system because the fuel and air mixture is compressed to about one-twentieth of its original volume, generating enough heat to ignite the fuel and air mixture without the need for an external spark [2], [3].

A diesel engine is very difficult to start in cold weather due to its low volatility of fuel. This difficulty arises from two main reasons mentioned in [2]: (3) Because diesel fuel is not as likely to explode in a collision and (4) Because diesel fuel is not very volatile, it is difficult to start a diesel engine in cold weather.
A diesel engine must be built much heavier than a gasoline engine due to the need for it to have enough strength to deal with the tighter compression of the fuel and air mixture. [2]
The property of diesel fuel that makes it less likely to explode in a collision is its oily consistency, which is described in [2] (TM-9-8000-principles-of-automotive-vehicles-1985.pdf, p.42).

A two-stroke cycle diesel requires a supercharger because it must force in the intake air and push out the burnt exhaust gases, as the movement of the piston is not such that it will accomplish this naturally. This requirement arises due to the fact that there are no intake valves in the engine design [2].

In a two-stroke cycle diesel engine, the exhaust valve is closed at top dead center. The intake ports are cut into the cylinder wall as in a two-stroke cycle gasoline engine.

A two-stroke cycle engine produces a power stroke every time the piston moves downward during one crankshaft revolution. However, this is different from producing twice as much power compared to a four-stroke cycle engine because the power stroke in a two-stroke diesel engine only lasts for part of the downstroke of the piston (from top dead center to bottom dead center). In contrast, a four-stroke diesel engine's power stroke lasts throughout the entire downstroke and upstroke. Therefore, even though there are twice as many power strokes per revolution in a two-stroke cycle engine, the actual duration of each power stroke is shorter, resulting in less overall power output compared to a four-stroke cycle engine [3].

A vehicle horn is normally operated through a relay rather than wired directly to its switch because the current draw of a horn is very high. This high current can damage the ignition switch and other components if the horn were directly controlled by the switch [2]. The relay allows for controlling the horn with lower currents, protecting both the relay and the ignition system from excessive load.

The tone and volume of a horn are adjusted by loosening the adjusting locknut and turning the adjusting nut. This very sensitive adjustment controls the current consumed by the horn, increasing the current increases the volume [2]. However, too much current will make the horn sputter and may lock the diaphragm [1].
If too much current goes through the light bulb filaments of a horn, for example, the filaments would overheat and burn out. Additionally, other electrical devices may be damaged [2].
In a dual horn installation, the air column formed by the projector and a spiral passage cast into the base of the horn controls the sound frequency of the low-pitch horn [17-10].

Vacuum-operated windshield wipers slow down or stop when a vehicle climbs a hill because the pressure in the intake manifold varies with engine loading. When the engine is loaded heavily, such as when climbing a hill, the speed of the wipers actually will stop due to the varying pressure in the intake manifold [17-14].

Early electric windshield wipers had a heavy electric current requirement that was placed on the vehicle's 6-volt electrical system. This problem was solved as 12-volt electrical systems became standard.

The park switch built into a windshield wiper motor is to provide power to the wiper motor long enough to return the wiper arms and blades to a retracted position whenever they are switched off by the operator. This can be inferred from [1] and [2], where it states that "the purpose of this switch is to provide power to the wiper motor long enough to return the wiper arms and blades to a retracted position whenever they are switched off by the operator."
Air-operated windshield wipers are used almost exclusively on heavy vehicles that are equipped with a compressed air supply system [1].

The rotary output of an electric wiper motor is transformed into the back-and-forth (reciprocating) motion of the wiper arms through a mechanism involving a worm gear and a crank. Specifically, the electric wiper motor drives a shaft via a worm gear that in turn moves a crank. The circular motion of this crank is then converted to reciprocating motion by means of a wiper transmission, which operates the wiper arms [1].
The auxiliary power receptacle is usually installed at the right-rear corner of the cab body, near the vehicle batteries [2].

The auxiliary power receptacle simplifies charging the batteries from an external source because it is wired in parallel with the battery, and only requires unscrewing the receptacle cap and plugging in the connector to make the connections. No disconnecting and reconnecting of the battery cable is necessary [2].

A large vehicle sometimes utilizes an air or electric horn at the rear that is actuated when the transmission is shifted to reverse. This purpose of this is to warn pedestrians when the vehicle is backing up [3].

A torque converter is used in an automatic transmission system instead of a driver-operated clutch because it does not require manual disengagement by the operator each time the vehicle is stopped. This feature reduces the workload on the driver and eliminates the need for frequent clutch engagement, which can be cumbersome and less efficient [2]. Additionally, the torque converter's ability to couple without interruption allows for smoother engine operation and a more comfortable driving experience due to its cushioning effect within the transmission system [2].

The pressure plate in an automatic transmission's multiple-disk clutch holds the stack of disks and plates together. It ensures that when hydraulic pressure is applied, the disks and plates are locked together to transmit torque by locking elements of the planetary gearsets to rotating members within the transmission [2].
The clutch piston seals serve to prevent the leakage of hydraulic pressure around the inner and outer circumferences of the clutch piston. [2]

The compound planetary drive train has largely replaced designs using two separate planetary gearsets due to its compactness and ability to provide two forward speeds, reverse, and neutral. [2] This arrangement combines two multiple-disk clutches and one brake band with a compound planetary gearset, which is described as "really two gearsets that are integrated together through the use of long and short pinions." [2]
When the gearshift lever is placed in neutral, the clutch and brake bands are released. The input shaft rotates freely and no torque is transmitted to the output shaft [3].

The hydraulic system of an automatic transmission routes oil through a remote cooler to remove excess heat generated in the transmission and torque converter, ensuring that all critical wearing surfaces are adequately lubricated. This is detailed in [3]. The cooler is located remotely from the transmission and operates by transferring the oil's latent heat to air via conduction through fins, which usually occurs in front of the engine radiator where it is subjected to airflow for efficient operation.

Besides planetary gearing, a cross-drive transmission contains a torque converter, steering mechanism, braking mechanism, and hydraulically operated clutches [2]. The brakes in these transmissions are foot-operated.
The driver of a tracked vehicle selects low range on a cross-drive transmission when extra driving torque is required, such as when pulling through heavy mud or sand. [2]

When the lockup clutch in the torque converter engages, the direct mechanical drive from the transmission input shaft is locked together with the turbine. This results in no speed reduction or torque multiplication occurring through the torque converter. The power path remains the same as shown in Figure 24-5 but without any speed reduction or torque increase due to the absence of the torque converter's hydraulic function [2].
When a tracked vehicle is driving straight ahead, no power passes through the steering system of a cross-drive transmission. [2]

During a steer in neutral range, the output ring gears remain stationary because they are both splined to the cross-drive shaft. The sun gears turn in opposite directions due to the differential arrangement being stationary during straight travel and the sun gears acting as reaction elements in the planetary sets [2].
